ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> All 117 participants were inverted against the frozen library.

> Pooling the 15 ×117 = 1755 posterior predictive p-values into a single KS test (D = 0.239, p ≈ 5 × 10 ⁸⁹) is not appropriate here, because the 15 statistics of one subject are strongly dependent, so ⁻ the degrees of freedom of that test are severely overestimated and the number is uninterpretable.

> Control-group composition: 86 of 117 participants had no SCID interview, and 9 subthreshold participants (mean BDI 23.1) were included in the control arm.

> Eyes-closed segments of 117 participants were successfully retrieved and preprocessed (mean 191 s, median 195 s).

> Three frequency priors -f logU(2.5, 16) (this work), logU (1, 20) and ∼ logU(4, 14) -are each used to build a 3 × 10⁴ library, and all 117 participants are re-inferred end to end with the same K and the same summary statistics; group effect sizes and the f_DMN-versus-HamD association are then compared.

Ethics approval statement:

> This study used only publicly available, de-identified data (OpenNeuro ds003478) and collected no new data; no new ethical approval was therefore required under our institutional rules.

Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). The sensitivity analysis confirms that the direction is robust, but a strict case-control design requires a larger sample." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.header: 2.6 What the mechanistic model adds over model-free spectral descriptors
table.expanded: On the question of discriminatory gain we give a direct interval estimate: between the best modelderived quantity (EI_AN, AUC 0.749) and the best descriptor (slope_SN, AUC 0.748) the pairedbootstrap AUC difference is 0.001, 95 % CI [-0.162, 0.156], p = 0.97 -not merely non-significant, but with an interval wide enough that even a real difference could not be resolved at this sample size.

table.header: 2.7 Symptom severity: model resonance frequency versus surface peak frequency
table.expanded: The model-inferred DMN resonance frequency correlated positively with HamD severity: ρ = 0.58 (bootstrap CI 0.27-0.79, p = 0.0007, n = 31), and the partial correlation controlling case status (whether MDD), age and sex was 0.54 (p = 0.003).

table.header: Composition of the HamD subsample and its sensitivity.
table.expanded: The association holds both within cases (ρ = 0.43, p = 0.048) and within non-cases (ρ = 0.80), and remains significant after controlling for case status (partial ρ = 0.54), so it cannot be attributed to diagnostic category; but it weakens to non-significance among the 11 current-MDD participants, so its robustness is limited by subsample size and requires replication in a larger sample.

data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 1116 files: 882 data, 146 code, 54 documentation, 34 materials.
-  We found 388 tabular data files and extracted 627 columns from 71 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 1 study group (ex1), plus 4 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
-  315 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass `local_path` to point at a local copy.
-  2 files read as a table but are not a usable rectangular dataset (9YGJC: LICENSE_DATA.txt: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; 9YGJC: results/H_runtime.csv: 75% of columns are free text, not variables). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 627 columns across 71 data files.
#### Issues Identified
10 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 71 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: This study used only publicly available, de-identified data (OpenNeuro ds003478) and collected no new data; no new ethical approval was therefore required under our institutional rules.
live_data_statements: All 117 participants were inverted against the frozen library.

Pooling the 15 ×117 = 1755 posterior predictive p-values into a single KS test (D = 0.239, p ≈ 5 × 10 ⁸⁹) is not appropriate here, because the 15 statistics of one subject are strongly dependent, so ⁻ the degrees of freedom of that test are severely overestimated and the number is uninterpretable.
Control-group composition: 86 of 117 participants had no SCID interview, and 9 subthreshold participants (mean BDI 23.1) were included in the control arm.
Eyes-closed segments of 117 participants were successfully retrieved and preprocessed (mean 191 s, median 195 s).

Three frequency priors -f logU(2.5, 16) (this work), logU (1, 20) and ∼ logU(4, 14) -are each used to build a 3 × 10⁴ library, and all 117 participants are re-inferred end to end with the same K and the same summary statistics; group effect sizes and the f_DMN-versus-HamD association are then compared.

text.text: Depression is widely thought to involve an imbalance between neuronal excitation and inhibition, but the idea has rarely been tested quantitatively at the level of macroscopic brain networks, because dynamical models are hard to fit to EEG spectra and fitting them person by person is prohibitively slow.
We present a complete, reproducible pipeline that makes such a test possible, and we report where it succeeds and where it does not.

Using eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants (22 with lifetime major depressive disorder, 95 without), we fitted a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model with an amortised Bayesian method, in which a single shared library of simulations serves every participant and reduces inference to milliseconds per person.
Depressed participants showed a consistent shift towards excitation in three core networks, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive.
The model's default-mode resonance frequency rose with symptom severity, whereas the conventional peak-frequency estimate computed from the same recordings did not.
We then asked what the model actually buys.
For distinguishing groups it did not outperform simple spectral measures, and its per-person low-frequency predictions were poor, so we restrict our claims accordingly.

A real-time state observer detected sudden shifts in the network's operating point within milliseconds, yet could not reconstruct the moment-to-moment state, a limit set by the model's intrinsic randomness rather than by our algorithm.

Finally, a dose-matched control showed that closed-loop stimulation is no more accurate than a fixed stimulus at the same dose, so we report the real-time feasibility of the loop without claiming an accuracy advantage.
The contribution of the paper is therefore a reusable, calibrated inference pipeline together with an explicit map of its limits, including negative findings that we deliberately kept as results.

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is one of the largest contributors to global disability, and its diagnosis still rests on symptom reports rather than on measurable properties of the brain [1] [2] [3].
text.formatted: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is one of the largest contributors to global disability, and its diagnosis still rests on symptom reports rather than on measurable properties of the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: A natural hope is that the disorder leaves a signature in large-scale brain dynamics, one that a clinician might eventually read off a short recording, and that the same signature would point to a mechanism [4].
text.formatted: A natural hope is that the disorder leaves a signature in large-scale brain dynamics, one that a clinician might eventually read off a short recording, and that the same signature would point to a mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Two decades of imaging and electrophysiology have produced many candidate markers, but most of them are statistical summaries: they separate groups in a particular sample without saying what, physically, has changed [5, 6].
text.formatted: Two decades of imaging and electrophysiology have produced many candidate markers, but most of them are statistical summaries: they separate groups in a particular sample without saying what, physically, has changed <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: A mechanistic account would need a generative model whose parameters carry biological meaning and whose values can be estimated for an individual person.
The most influential mechanistic account is the excitation/inhibition (E/I) imbalance hypothesis [7].
text.formatted: The most influential mechanistic account is the excitation/inhibition (E/I) imbalance hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy reports reduced cortical GABA and altered glutamate/glutamine in depression [8] [9] [10] [11]; the rapid antidepressant action of ketamine points to glutamatergic signalling [12]; and a recent combined MRS-EEG study links gamma oscillations to E/I balance in depressed patients [13].
text.formatted: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy reports reduced cortical GABA and altered glutamate/glutamine in depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>; the rapid antidepressant action of ketamine points to glutamatergic signalling <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>; and a recent combined MRS-EEG study links gamma oscillations to E/I balance in depressed patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: The hypothesis is therefore attractive, but the evidence is cellular and regional.
Whether the E/I ratio of macroscopic networks is shifted in depression has not been settled, largely because it is not directly observable in scalp EEG.
Non-invasive proxies exist and are widely used.

The aperiodic exponent of the power spectrum has been proposed as an index of E/I balance, on the grounds that the interplay of excitation and inhibition shapes the spectral slope [14, 15]; it can be estimated robustly by separating periodic from aperiodic components [16] and it tracks behavioural and clinical states [17] [18] [19].
text.formatted: The aperiodic exponent of the power spectrum has been proposed as an index of E/I balance, on the grounds that the interplay of excitation and inhibition shapes the spectral slope <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>; it can be estimated robustly by separating periodic from aperiodic components <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> and it tracks behavioural and clinical states <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: EEG markers of depression, including alpha power and individual alpha peak frequency, have been reviewed extensively [20] [21] [22], and alpha peak frequency is a stable individual trait [23] [24] [25] [26].
text.formatted: EEG markers of depression, including alpha power and individual alpha peak frequency, have been reviewed extensively <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>, and alpha peak frequency is a stable individual trait <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: These descriptors are easy to compute and statistically convenient, but they are not parameters of a mechanism: a change in the exponent or in peak frequency can be produced by many different underlying changes, and the descriptors carry no way of predicting how the system would respond to a perturbation.
Biophysical network models offer the complementary route.

The Wilson-Cowan (WC) model, the canonical mean-field description of coupled excitatory and inhibitory populations, has parameters that map directly onto synaptic coupling and drive [27, 28], and it has been extended into neural-mass models of EEG and MEG spectra [29] [30] [31], into dynamic causal modelling (DCM) of evoked and resting-state data [32] [33] [34] [35] [36], and into large-scale simulators [37, 38].

text.text: The obstacle is inferential rather than conceptual.
Two practical obstacles have limited this route at cohort scale.
First, the prior is ill posed: when excitatory self-coupling, inhibitory weight and tonic drive are sampled independently, most of the prior volume falls into saturated or unstable regimes.

Over exactly the parameter ranges used here, only 2.4 % of independent draws pass the stability screen and 61.2 % have a negative determinant of the excitatoryinhibitory sub-Jacobian, so the inversion is dominated by the prior rather than by the data; a construction that samples the operating point and the rhythm frequency explicitly raises the acceptance rate to 30.3 % and removes the saddles altogether.
Second, inference is expensive per subject: likelihood-based schemes such as DCM optimise each subject separately, which is impractical for hundreds of recordings.

Simulation-based inference (SBI) offers an amortised alternative, in which one simulated library is generated once and then serves every new subject, and it has become a standard tool across the physical and life sciences [44] [45] [46] [47] [48] [49].

text.text: A third motivation is therapeutic.

Rhythmic and closed-loop stimulation can entrain or disrupt ongoing oscillations [60, 61], non-invasive stimulation is increasingly combined with electrophysiological read-out [62], deep brain stimulation is an established treatment for refractory depression [63], and closing the loop between measurement and stimulation has produced clinical benefit in essential tremor and in age-related cognitive decline [64, 65].

text.text: A controller needs a real-time estimate of the system state, which is precisely what a state-space formulation of the WC model provides [66] [67] [68] [69] [70] [71].
text.formatted: A controller needs a real-time estimate of the system state, which is precisely what a state-space formulation of the WC model provides <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[66]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">[67]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[68]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[69]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[70]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[71]</ref>.

text.text: Whether that estimate is good enough, and whether closing the loop is actually better than a well-chosen fixed stimulus, are empirical questions rather than matters of design philosophy.

We therefore ask four questions of a single dataset of eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants. (i) Can the WC prior be made well posed, so that every draw corresponds to a stable network with a controlled rhythm frequency?
(ii) Can the parameters, and the quantities derived from them, be inferred for a whole cohort from one shared simulation library, and are those answers calibrated?
(iii) Do the inferred E/I balance and rhythm frequencies differ in depression, and do they add anything to simple spectral descriptors?
(iv) What are the limits: how much of the latent state is observable at all, does closing the stimulation loop help once the dose is matched, and which statistics does the model fail to reproduce?
Section 2 answers these questions in turn, Section 3 discusses them, and Section 4 gives the materials and methods.

We have deliberately kept the boundaries of the method as first-class results: the negative and limiting findings (no discriminative advantage over spectral descriptors, a tracking limit imposed by the model's own stochasticity, a band-limited fit, and the absence of any accuracy advantage from closing the stimulation loop) are reported alongside the positive ones, because they define what the model may be used to say.

The analysis is organised so that the validity of each claim is established before the claim is made: the estimator is calibrated on synthetic data, the derived quantities are recovered against known truth, and the conclusions are then tested against alternative control definitions, an alternative prior specification and a dose-matched stimulation control.

The validation above covers the 15 free parameters, whereas the biological conclusions rest on the E/I balance index, the inhibitory loop gain, the resonance frequencies and the drive offset.

One point deserves particular attention: the resonance frequency f_i is not a free parameter -it is the target used to solve for wEI_i when the prior is constructed, and it is afterwards re-derived from the posterior samples through the linearised Jacobian (code/04_fit.py::_res_freq).
The posterior of f_i may therefore be dominated by the prior, and has to be calibrated on its own.

text.text: Three points deserve emphasis.

First, the resonance frequencies recover best: coverage 1.00 for f_DMN with a true-value correlation of 0.84 (f_SN 0.99/0.88, f_AN 0.96/0.86), so although their contraction is only 0.11-0.22 their posterior is not prior-dominated -it correlates strongly with the truth and its intervals are correctly calibrated.

text.text: Three points stand out.

First, separating the un-interviewed from the interviewed non-cases leaves the effect sizes in the same direction and of the same order, so the conclusion does not rest on the heterogeneity of the control arm.

Readers are entitled to ask what the model buys.

We compared five model-derived quantities with ten model-free spectral descriptors (aperiodic exponents, alpha peak frequencies, alpha relative powers, total power) on the same footing (Table 8; the full 15-marker panel is shipped as supporting information), and we add bootstrap intervals for every quantity and for each AUC [76, 77].

text.text: On the question of discriminatory gain we give a direct interval estimate: between the best modelderived quantity (EI_AN, AUC 0.749) and the best descriptor (slope_SN, AUC 0.748) the pairedbootstrap AUC difference is 0.001, 95 % CI [-0.162, 0.156], p = 0.97 -not merely non-significant, but with an interval wide enough that even a real difference could not be resolved at this sample size.
We therefore make no claim that the model outperforms spectral descriptors.

What the model provides is (i) parameters with explicit mechanistic meaning rather than statistical summaries, (ii) a calibrated posterior uncertainty for every individual, which descriptors do not provide, (iii) the basis for the real-time state observer and control layer of Sections 2.8-2.9, and (iv) an association with the symptom dimension (Section 2.7).

The association is therefore neither purely within-case nor a clean case-control comparison.
The subsample results are:

The association holds both within cases (ρ = 0.43, p = 0.048) and within non-cases (ρ = 0.80), and remains significant after controlling for case status (partial ρ = 0.54), so it cannot be attributed to diagnostic category; but it weakens to non-significance among the 11 current-MDD participants, so its robustness is limited by subsample size and requires replication in a larger sample.

On group differences in the model resonance frequency: f_DMN is essentially identical between MDD and controls (10.07 vs 9.99 Hz, g = 0.04, p = 0.79), and f_SN and f_AN are if anything slightly lower in MDD.

The frequencies are therefore not a between-group marker but a quantity associated with the continuous symptom load; this section and Section 2.5 do not conflict, because diagnostic category and symptom load are two different contrasts, and the model parameters are associated only with the latter.
Note also that f is unit-dependent: f_i is derived analytically from the linearised Jacobian and therefore depends directly on the fixed τ_E = 10 ms and τ_I = 20 ms.

As shown in the τ-sensitivity table (S2 Data), scaling τ by 0.75-1.25 makes the mean of f_DMN change strictly as 1/τ (13.34 Hz at ×0.75), while ρ(f_DMN, HamD) = 0.579 and the group effect g = 0.04 are completely unchanged across the whole range.
In other words: the absolute value of f is τ-dependent (a known cost), but its association with severity is not.
Three points deserve emphasis.

First, the model resonance frequency is comparable in magnitude to the simplest descriptor (alpha relative power) in its HamD association -the model does not win -but the model delivers a reusable frequency parameter (the same quantity is used in the group contrast, the uncertainty quantification and the state observer), whereas alpha relative power is only a descriptive summary.

Second, the non-parametric peak frequency fails where the parametric one succeeds: the peak is a point estimate contaminated by the 1/f background and by peak width, and the model's explicit separation of resonance frequency from damping preserves the association with severity.
Third, the EI_DMN association with HamD is negative, opposite in sign to its BDI association (different subsamples); we do not offer a mechanistic reading of this inconsistency.
We first quantified a decisive quantity: the predictability of the latent state itself.

Simulating two trajectories with the same drive, the same parameters and only a different random seed gave a median correlation of 0.97 (mean 0.84), i.e. most of the trajectory variance comes from the shared deterministic response to the drive; for a few near-saturated subjects the between-realisation correlation dropped below 0.4, where the model's intrinsic stochasticity is of the same order as the signal.

text.text: Two points stand out.
The effective sample size stayed near 1000/1500: particle degeneracy would show up as an ESS collapsing to single digits, so the accuracy limit reflects limited information, not numerical failure.
And the profiled observation noise (0.165) systematically exceeded the truth (0.075), because the filter's predictive spread absorbs the model's intrinsic state fluctuations.
It must be said directly: the mean skill score is only 0.045, which is tantamount to "the state cannot be reconstructed moment by moment", not to "tracking works well".
The improvement over the mean-only baseline is marginal.

A separate oracle-noise ablation (unavailable in practice; an upper bound) shows that even with the true observation noise the E-state correlation rises only from 0.63 to 0.73 (median 0.87) and the skill score from 0.05 to 0.23: sample-by-sample tracking is bounded at 0.7-0.9 and cannot be pushed to near-perfection by better algorithms.

For four of the sixteen pseudo-subjects the skill score stayed negative even with the true σ, because their trajectories had almost no variance (baseline RMSE 0.008-0.22) and hence almost no trackable information.

In sharp contrast, the observer detected operating-point shifts (a step in the drive) almost immediately: the median latency to first cross "pre-step mean + 2 SD" was 0.008 s (mean 0.013 s, range 0.004-0.032 s), with ESS between 620 and 1013 throughout.
That is precisely the quantity a closed-loop controller needs -not the reconstruction of every moment, but the fastest possible detection that the state has left its target.

On five real subjects, driving the observer with each subject's ABC posterior-median parameters produced stable, convergent filtering: median ESS 478-836/1500, resampling rate 0.40-0.84, and profiled observation noise at the lower edge of the grid (0.01-0.02), indicating that the fluctuation time scale of the real regional signals matches the model's E dynamics closely.

The three stimulation conditions (no stimulation, fixed-amplitude open loop, closed loop) share the same noise realisation, as such closed-loop designs conventionally do [62, 66]; the first 20 % of each trial is unperturbed and its mean defines the control target, after which a pathological drop of 0.55 in tonic drive is applied (upper half of Table 12, Figure 9C).
text.formatted: The three stimulation conditions (no stimulation, fixed-amplitude open loop, closed loop) share the same noise realisation, as such closed-loop designs conventionally do <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">[62,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">66]</ref>; the first 20 % of each trial is unperturbed and its mean defines the control target, after which a pathological drop of 0.55 in tonic drive is applied (upper half of Table <ref type="table">12</ref>, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">9C</ref>).

text.text: A fixed open-loop amplitude at u = 0.55 -exactly the pathological drive reduction -would implicitly encode prior knowledge of the perturbation amplitude, and a comparison against such a baseline conflates "feedback" with "dose".

We therefore also solve for an open-loop amplitude from each trial's closed-loop dose (u = dose / 96 s), so that the two arms deliver the same dose, and we add an open-loop dose gradient at u = 0.10, 0.20 and 0.35 to trace the complete doseerror curve.

Dose-matched comparison: at equal dose, the closed loop (0.139) and the constant open loop (0.140) show no statistical difference in steady-state error (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.12); the same holds when restricted to the 7 trials on which the closed loop actually stimulated (0.151 vs 0.152, p = 0.30).
The apparent advantage of the closed loop -a 38 % error reduction for 34 % of the dose, i.e.

1.6 times the efficiency per unit dose -therefore does not survive dose matching -that factor of 1.6 came from a comparison against a deliberately near-ceiling fixed amplitude, not from feedback itself.
Two things the closed loop demonstrably provides in this simulation remain.

The first is real-time feasibility: the particle filter runs at 18.2 % of real time and the observer detects an operating-point step with a median latency of 8 ms, so a model of this size fits inside the closed-loop budget.

The second is that the dose becomes state-adaptive: across the 12 trials the closed-loop dose ranged from 0 to 76 (mean 18.0), and on 5 trials it delivered 0 (Figure 10B), whereas the open loop applied the same dose every time.
text.formatted: The second is that the dose becomes state-adaptive: across the 12 trials the closed-loop dose ranged from 0 to 76 (mean 18.0), and on 5 trials it delivered 0 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">10B</ref>), whereas the open loop applied the same dose every time.

text.text: We must be honest, however, that those 5 zero-dose trials are not "correct restraint" but a failure of the controller to recognise the perturbation: the controller uses only prior-centre parameters and does not know the subject's true parameters, so the filter estimate is pulled towards a healthy operating point and the target is judged to have been met.

The more accurate statement is therefore that the potential of closing the loop is to turn the dose into a state-adaptive quantity and to remove the need for prior knowledge of the perturbation amplitude, but that the controller designed here is not sufficient to convert that potential into an accuracy advantage; the improvement path is to let the controller use the subject's own posterior parameters or to identify the perturbation online.
The calibration of Sections 2.2-2.3 concerns parameter recovery (prior self-consistency on synthetic data).

Real data require a second check: for each subject we drew 48 parameter sets from the posterior by weight, simulated, computed the 15 statistics, and asked whether the observed value falls inside its 95 % posterior predictive interval (Figure 11).
text.formatted: Real data require a second check: for each subject we drew 48 parameter sets from the posterior by weight, simulated, computed the 15 statistics, and asked whether the observed value falls inside its 95 % posterior predictive interval (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_11">11</ref>).

text.text: Pooling the 15 ×117 = 1755 posterior predictive p-values into a single KS test (D = 0.239, p ≈ 5 × 10 ⁸⁹) is not appropriate here, because the 15 statistics of one subject are strongly dependent, so ⁻ the degrees of freedom of that test are severely overestimated and the number is uninterpretable.
We therefore use: per-statistic coverage with exact (Clopper-Pearson) intervals, per-statistic KS uniformity tests (BH-corrected), a subject-level clustered bootstrap and a Monte-Carlo test.
Table 13 gives the perstatistic outcome, and the same quantities are shown as coverage and departure-from-uniformity panels in Figure 11.

text.text: The result is a restrictive but actionable finding: mean per-statistic coverage is only 0.758 (subject-level clustered bootstrap 95 % CI 0.725-0.791; median per-subject coverage 0.80), and 12 of the 15 per-statistic p-value distributions depart significantly from uniformity (BH q < 0.05).
text.formatted: The result is a restrictive but actionable finding: mean per-statistic coverage is only 0.758 (subject-level clustered bootstrap 95 % CI 0.725-0.791; median per-subject coverage 0.80), and 12 of the 15 per-statistic p-value distributions depart significantly from uniformity (BH q < 0.05).

text.text: The structure is clear: • Inter-regional imaginary coherency: iCOH_DMN_SN (0.949) is compatible with nominal; but iCOH_DMN_AN (0.991) and iCOH_SN_AN (1.000) show over-coverage, i.e. prediction intervals that are too wide and therefore under-discriminative -also a form of misfit, invisible in a coverage number alone, which is why we report the KS test as well.
• Alpha band and DMN_delta: AN_alpha 0.889 (KS q = 0.106, marginally usable), DMN_delta 0.846, SN_alpha 0.812.
• Theta/delta/beta relative powers are systematically too narrow: AN_theta 0.410, SN_theta 0.581, DMN_beta 0.650.

The reading is that the model class explicitly parameterises an alpha resonance and inter-regional coupling, so per-subject predictions of those statistics are trustworthy, whereas low-frequency (theta/delta) and high-frequency (beta) relative powers are not directly constrained by the model's mechanism and are not reproduced subject by subject.
This bounds the inference: the E/I-derived quantities, resonance frequencies and coupling indices are reportable, while the claim that the model reproduces a participant's full spectrum is not.

We treat this as an actionable result, because it identifies where the model must be extended -for instance with slow inhibitory adaptation or a thalamo-cortical loop to constrain the theta band -and we confirm with a random split of the cohort into halves (coverage 0.764 vs 0.753) that the verdict is stable in sample.
>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Discussion</head>

text.text: In eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants, amortised Bayesian inversion of a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model gave three headline results.

First, depression was accompanied by a shift towards excitation in all three networks studied, the default-mode network, the salience network and an anterior frontopolar node, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive; the intervals of five derived quantities excluded zero, and the direction survived alternative definitions of the control group and a symptom-dimension contrast.

This is what the E/I imbalance hypothesis predicts at the macroscopic level [7] [8] [9], and it is the first cohort-level test of that prediction to rest on a model whose derived quantities have been calibrated individually.
text.formatted: This is what the E/I imbalance hypothesis predicts at the macroscopic level <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>, and it is the first cohort-level test of that prediction to rest on a model whose derived quantities have been calibrated individually.

text.text: Second, the model-inferred default-mode rhythm frequency rose with symptom severity, while the conventional alpha peak frequency measured from the same recordings did not (partial rho = 0.54 controlling case status); the association is not significant among the 11 participants with current MDD, so its robustness is limited by subsample size and it requires replication in a larger sample [20, 22].
text.formatted: Second, the model-inferred default-mode rhythm frequency rose with symptom severity, while the conventional alpha peak frequency measured from the same recordings did not (partial rho = 0.54 controlling case status); the association is not significant among the 11 participants with current MDD, so its robustness is limited by subsample size and it requires replication in a larger sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>.

text.text: Third, we mapped the boundaries.

At the state level, sample-by-sample tracking is bounded by the model's intrinsic stochasticity (r about 0.63, with an oraclenoise upper bound of 0.73), whereas sudden shifts of the operating point are detected within milliseconds, which is the quantity a controller actually needs.
Closed-loop stimulation, compared against a dosematched open loop, gave no accuracy advantage, so we claim real-time feasibility and the potential of a state-adaptive dose, but not an accuracy gain.
A constructive fix for the ill-posed prior, with a reproducible metric.

Independent sampling of gains leaves only 2.4 % of draws usable and makes 61.2 % of them saddles; the stable frequency parameterisation raises the acceptance rate to 30.3 % and reduces the saddle fraction to 0.
Calibrated amortised inference.

One library of 1.2 × 10⁵ simulations served 117 participants at an amortisation ratio of ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵, with coverage near 0.95 for K ≥ 250 and N ≥ 3 × 10⁴, and with conclusions that do not drift with the hyper-parameters; the conclusion is additionally verified under three independent frequency priors, end to end.

We also report the negative result that the locallinear adjustment inflates the bias to +4.5 and the coverage to 0.31, which is why it is off by default, and which illustrates the general point that a regression-adjusted estimator need not improve on the plain one [50, 72].
text.formatted: We also report the negative result that the locallinear adjustment inflates the bias to +4.5 and the coverage to 0.31, which is why it is off by default, and which illustrates the general point that a regression-adjusted estimator need not improve on the plain one <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">72]</ref>.

text.text: Although the resonance frequencies contract only by 0.11-0.22, their recovery coverage is 0.96-1.00 with correlations of 0.84-0.88; the loop gain has a negative contraction and is therefore restricted to group-level statements and never interpreted individually.
The mean skill score is 0.045, and we state explicitly that sample-by-sample reconstruction is not achievable; an oracle-noise ablation pins the ceiling at 0.7-0.9.
The apparent dose efficiency of closed-loop stimulation does not survive a dose-matched comparison.
We report it as a negative result rather than retaining a "positive" conclusion that depends on an inappropriate baseline. 6.
text.formatted: We report it as a negative result rather than retaining a "positive" conclusion that depends on an inappropriate baseline. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref>.

text.text: A band-limited adequacy statement.

Posterior predictive checks show well-calibrated statistics (iCOH, alpha power) coexisting with systematic misfit (theta/delta/beta relative power), which delimits what this model class may be used to claim.
The E/I imbalance hypothesis predicts excitation dominance in depression [7] [8] [9].
text.formatted: The E/I imbalance hypothesis predicts excitation dominance in depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Our results are consistent with it at the level of macroscopic network dynamics, and they connect the spectroscopy literature to EEG: if cortical E/I shifts, the network-level signature should be a change in balance and in the strength of inhibitory feedback, which is what we observe.

The non-parametric route to E/I from field potentials [14, 15] provides the natural benchmark, and we find that the two families have comparable discriminative power under a common criterion, a result that should temper the assumption that mechanism buys accuracy.
text.formatted: The non-parametric route to E/I from field potentials <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref> provides the natural benchmark, and we find that the two families have comparable discriminative power under a common criterion, a result that should temper the assumption that mechanism buys accuracy.

text.text: Spectral parameterisation tools [16] and the aperiodic-exponent literature [17] [18] [19] are complementary rather than competing: they describe the spectrum without committing to a mechanism, and our band-limited misfit, in which theta, delta and beta relative powers are not reproduced, says that the two should be combined rather than opposed.

text.text: Within the modelling literature, this work sits between the neural-mass and whole-brain traditions.

The WC model and its descendants supply the local dynamics [27] [28] [29] [30] [31]; DCM concentrates on a small number of subjects with subject-specific optimisation and model comparison [32] [33] [34] [35] [36] 78]; and whole-brain modelling has begun to address clinical stratification and the role of the E/I ratio [37] [38] [39] 42, 43].

text.text: Our contribution is not a new model but a scalable inversion of an existing one, together with the calibration evidence that amortised inference requires.
Methodologically this is an instance of simulation-based inference at cohort scale [49, 55], and it inherits the validation obligations of that field [58, 59, 72, 73, 79, 80].

text.text: The closed-loop component connects to two literatures.

Non-invasive rhythmic stimulation can entrain cortical oscillations [60] [61] [62], and closed-loop paradigms have produced clinical gains in essential tremor and in working memory [64, 65], while invasive stimulation is established in refractory depression [63].

text.text: Control-group composition: 86 of 117 participants had no SCID interview, and 9 subthreshold participants (mean BDI 23.1) were included in the control arm.
The sensitivity analysis confirms that the direction is robust, but a strict case-control design requires a larger sample.
Restricted population: the cohort is 18-24 years old, so the conclusions are confined to late adolescence and early adulthood.

Spatial reduction: only 12 channels were downloaded (FZ, P1, PZ, P2, FC1, FCZ, FC2, AF3, AF4, O1, OZ, O2, used as network proxies plus an occipital reference); no average reference was applied, no source reconstruction was performed and no lead field was modelled; averaging within a network ignores heterogeneity.

Representing the third network by AF3/AF4 stretches construct validityits anterior part is available, but the parietal nodes of the canonical frontoparietal control network are missing (P1/PZ/P2 were assigned to the DMN).
We therefore relabel it the anterior frontopolar node (AN) and present its results only as evidence about an anterior network [83].

text.text: Identifiability: wII and the inter-regional couplings are weakly identified, and the loop gain has a non-positive contraction, so its individual values are not interpreted.

Model simplifications: τ, θ and σ are fixed; there are no conduction delays and no thalamo-cortical loop; the absolute value of f scales with τ (S2 Data); and the closed-loop results remain simulation evidence without validation in real stimulation [56].

text.text: The absolute scale of the observation is not identifiable: EEG amplitude is arbitrary and the observation gain and noise are partly collinear, so the absolute level of the latent state cannot be recovered from a single recording.

We therefore standardise each signal to the subject's own model E fluctuation scale and centre it on its operating point, which makes the observer an estimator of deviations from the operating point, and take the control target from the measured pre-perturbation operating point. 10.
text.formatted: We therefore standardise each signal to the subject's own model E fluctuation scale and centre it on its operating point, which makes the observer an estimator of deviations from the operating point, and take the control target from the measured pre-perturbation operating point. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref>.

text.text: Constructed nature of the synthetic validation: the observer benchmark injects a known slow drive, so it tests whether a state that does carry information can be tracked, not whether all resting-state dynamics are explained by this model.

Further limitation of the closed-loop control: a fixed open-loop amplitude u = 0.55 equal to the perturbation amplitude implicitly encodes prior knowledge of that amplitude; if the perturbation amplitude varies between trials the controller would have to be retuned.
The dose-matched comparison exposes the baseline dependence of the efficiency claim, but we did not run an experiment with a mismatched perturbation amplitude, which we leave to future work.

We established and validated a complete, reproducible pipeline -three-region Wilson-Cowan modelling, a stable frequency-parameterised prior, amortised ABC inversion, group statistics with bootstrap uncertainty and a power analysis, posterior predictive adequacy checks at the subject level, real-time state estimation and closed-loop stimulation simulation -and we report three of its boundaries: identifiability (gains and loop gain are weakly identified, whereas the resonance frequencies are well calibrated), observability (tracking capped at 0.7-0.9 while operating-point detection takes 8 ms) and adequacy (lowfrequency band powers are not reproduced).
Applied to public depression EEG, the method reveals a consistent E/I shift and elevated loop gain across three core networks, plus a severity-related network resonance frequency.
What is directly reusable is the modular structure of the pipeline, its calibration evidence, and the limits it makes explicit, including one negative conclusion that we kept.
We see the honest reporting of those limits as part of the contribution rather than as a caveat [38, 49, 82].

text.text: Data.

OpenNeuro dataset ds003478 (*EEG: Depression rest*) [89], containing resting-state EEG of depressed and control participants in alternating ~66 s eyes-closed/eyes-open blocks at 500 Hz, 64 EEG + 2 EOG channels, with BDI, STAI, SCID and HamD clinical scales.
text.formatted: OpenNeuro dataset ds003478 (*EEG: Depression rest*) <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">[89]</ref>, containing resting-state EEG of depressed and control participants in alternating ~66 s eyes-closed/eyes-open blocks at 500 Hz, 64 EEG + 2 EOG channels, with BDI, STAI, SCID and HamD clinical scales.

text.text: To keep the download tractable (HTTP range requests) we selected 12 channels in advance as network proxies: FZ, P1, PZ, P2 (DMN), FC1, FCZ, FC2 (SN/dACC), AF3, AF4 (anterior frontopolar), and O1, OZ, O2 (occipital reference, used for the aperiodic exponent and peak-frequency descriptors).
This choice was made before the data were inspected, but it does limit spatial resolution (Section 3.4, item 6).
Eyes-closed segments of 117 participants were successfully retrieved and preprocessed (mean 191 s, median 195 s).

The archive stores the raw data in a time-major layout (not the conventional channel-major EEGLAB layout); reading it as channel-major introduces spectral comb artefacts at 15/30/45 Hz, so we parse it as time-major.

Preprocessing (code/02_preprocess.py, built on the MNE-Python, NumPy and SciPy stacks [84] [85] [86] and organised along BIDS lines [83]): (1) eyes-open/closed decoding from event values (odd = closed), keeping eyes-closed segments only; (2) despiking by robust median/MAD z-scores with linear interpolation of flagged runs up to 25 samples; (3) ocular regression on HEOG including ±60 ms lagged copies; (4) 0.5-45 Hz zero-phase FIR band-pass plus a 60 Hz notch; (5) resampling 500 → 250 Hz; (6) rejection of 1 s windows whose power exceeds median + 6•MAD.

text.text: Model and data are summarised by the same function, giving a 15-dimensional vector: • 12 band log relative powers: log(band power / broadband 1-30 Hz) for δ(1-4), θ(4-8), α(8-13) and β(13-30) Hz in each of the three regions; • 3 alpha-band imaginary coherences: mean |Im coherency| over 8-13 Hz for DMN-SN, DMN-AN and SN-AN, which are insensitive to zero-lag volume conduction.
|Im coherency| carries a positive finite-sample bias √(1/(πL)) with L the number of averaged segments; the analytic null value is subtracted from both model and data.

text.text: A single prior-predictive library of N = 1.2 × 10⁵ pairs (θ_i, s_i) is generated once.

For each subject, distances are computed in MAD-standardised summary space, the K = 250 nearest neighbours are retained, and the Epanechnikov kernel w_i = 1 -(d_i/d_(K))² defines the weighted posterior sample {θ_k, w_k}.

The regression adjustment of Beaumont and colleagues [45, 50] is off by default: on 80 pseudo-subjects it raises the wEE bias to +4.51 with an MSE/variance of 5.03 and a coverage of 0.31 (Table 4), whereas the plain weighted-neighbour posterior is calibrated (bias ≈ 0, MSE/variance ≤ 1).

text.text: Eighty pseudo-subjects drawn from the prior are inverted with the identical pipeline, reporting bias, MSE/variance, correlation and 95 % coverage, in the spirit of simulation-based calibration [58, 59, 79]; the same battery is applied to every derived quantity (EI_i, f_i, loop gain, drive offset) as well (Table 3).

text.text: Hyper-parameter sensitivity.

On a fixed set of pseudo-subjects (fixed seed) the recovery validation is repeated for K {60, 120, 250, 500, 1000} and for libraries subsampled to N {3 × 10⁴, 6 × 10⁴, 1.2 × ∈ ∈ 10⁵}; in parallel, the group effect sizes of the real cohort are recomputed at each K to test whether the biological conclusion drifts.
Prior-specification robustness.

Three frequency priors -f logU(2.5, 16) (this work), logU (1, 20) and ∼ logU(4, 14) -are each used to build a 3 × 10⁴ library, and all 117 participants are re-inferred end to end with the same K and the same summary statistics; group effect sizes and the f_DMN-versus-HamD association are then compared.

text.text: Performance.

We measure (i) the cost of one prior-predictive simulation (average over 512 draws), (ii) the extrapolated build time of the 1.2 × 10⁵ library on one and eight cores, (iii) the per-subject and fullcohort ABC query times, and (iv) the particle filter's compute time per second of data (1500 particles, 20 s of synthetic data).
The amortisation ratio is the library build time divided by the per-subject inference time.
All times are wall-clock and are taken from the reference run recorded in S8 Data.

Derived quantities: the E/I balance index EI_i = log10(wEE_i/wEI_i); the inhibitory loop gain g_loop = √(wIE•wII); the operating-point drive offset Δ; the per-region analytic resonance frequencies f_i; and the six inter-regional couplings C_ij.

To ask what the model adds, ten model-free descriptors (aperiodic exponents in three regions, alpha peak frequencies, alpha relative powers, total power) are compared with five model-derived quantities under a common criterion: group Hedges g, AUC (converted from the Mann-Whitney U), FDR-corrected q, and each marker's Spearman correlation with HamD/BDI, including bootstrap intervals and within-family FDR [26, 79].

text.text: We also report a paired-bootstrap interval for the AUC difference between the best model-derived quantity and the best descriptor.
For each subject, 48 parameter sets are drawn from the posterior (the 250 weighted neighbours) by weight, simulated, and reduced to the 15 statistics.

For each statistic we test whether the observed value falls inside the 95 % posterior predictive interval (with exact intervals for the coverage [90]) and run a perstatistic KS uniformity test (BH-corrected).

A pooled KS test over 15 × 117 dependent p-values is avoided here, because its degrees of freedom would be severely overstated [58, 59, 80].

text.text: The step is complementary to the recovery validation of Section 4.5: the latter tests the estimator's calibration on synthetic data, the former the model's adequacy on real data.
The state is x = (E_1..3, I_1..3); the dynamics are the WC equations at the subject's posterior-median parameters, and the observation is the three regional signals y_t = g•E_t + n_t.

The key design choice is to make the latent state genuinely trackable: without an input the model sits essentially at its fixed point, so any observer would be evaluating noise fitting rather than tracking, an uninformative benchmark.

Synthetic validation therefore injects a known slow drive (0.12-0.65 Hz sinusoid, amplitude 0.15-0.60) so that E_t follows a structured deterministic trajectory, with 40 % relative observation noise added.

The signal is expressed in latent units (g = 1) and only the observation noise σ is profiled -by maximising the one-step predictive log-likelihood on the first 25 % of the record, with the Gaussian normalising constant included (otherwise σ saturates at the grid's upper bound) -and then frozen for the held-out window.
The bootstrap filter [67] [68] [69] [70] uses 1500 particles initialised at the model's own operating point (E*, I*).
text.formatted: The bootstrap filter <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">[67]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[68]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[69]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[70]</ref> uses 1500 particles initialised at the model's own operating point (E*, I*).

text.text: Reported metrics: state RMSE, skill = 1 -RMSE/baseline relative to the mean-only baseline, E/I state correlations, ESS and resampling rate.
Detection latency is the time from a drive step until the filtered estimate first crosses "pre-step mean + 2 SD".
A separate oracle-σ ablation bounds tracking performance.

Because real EEG has neither ground truth nor an absolute scale, each subject's signals are first standardised to that subject's model E fluctuation scale and centred on its operating point E* (with g = 1) before σ is profiled.
Three conditions (no stimulation, fixed-amplitude open loop, closed loop) share one noise realisation.

The first 20 % of each trial is unperturbed and its mean defines the healthy operating point used as the control target; a pathological drop of 0.55 in tonic drive is then applied, and the conditions differ only in how they stimulate.
The observation is g•E plus noise (g = 8) and the target is the mean excitatory activity across regions.

The closed loop runs the particle filter (800 particles) on the most recent 0.6 s of observation every 0.1 s and sets the stimulation amplitude to u = clip(2.5•(E*_healthy -Ê), 0, 0.8); the open loop applies a fixed amplitude after the perturbation.
The controller uses only prior-centre parameters and does not know the subject's true parameters.

We compare the steady-state error (final 20 s), the dose ∫|u|dt and the fraction of time within ±10 % of the target, using paired Wilcoxon tests, and report the error reduction per unit dose; the controller and the dose-matching logic follow standard feedback-systems practice [91].

text.text: For each trial the open-loop amplitude is solved from the closed-loop dose as u_match = dose_closed / (0.8 • T_total), so that the two arms deliver the same dose; an open-loop gradient at u = 0.10, 0.20 and 0.35 is added to trace the dose-error curve (code/17_dose_matched.py).
All conditions reuse the same per-trial seeds, so the noise realisations are paired.
